newsitem.title: UK: EU Commissioner says no going back on EMU.
newsitem.headline: EU Commissioner says no going back on EMU.

text.p: The political will behind a single European currency is rock solid and the project has passed the point of no return, European Union Commissioner for monetary affairs Yves Thibault de Silguy said on Wednesday.
"The process now is irreversible and we are within sight of the finishing line," he said in a telephone interview with BBC radio. "We are past the non-return point."

"If we have problems, it is natural because we are working on the details of the project. But the political will is rock solid and I am sure all the governments (will) take all the necessary measures to respect the timetable of the conditions."
France's new socialist government has said it needs time to study the stability pact, an integral part of EU plans for economic and monetary union (EMU).
The pact, agreed in principle in Dublin in December, is designed to keep EU budgets in order after EMU is launched on January 1, 1999.
De Silguy said all EU governments had agreed that the euro would be a reality on January 1, 1999 in line with the timetable laid down in the Maastricht Treaty.
This message had been clear at this week's meeting of EU finance ministers in Luxembourg.
"No-one questioned the deadline, no-one questioned the objective," de Silguy said.

There was no question about the new French government's commitment to monetary union. "The first thing (Finance Minister Dominique) Strauss-Kahn said last Monday was to confirm his determination to respect the January 1, 1999 deadline," the commissioner added.
He said it was natural that the new French government of Prime Minister Lionel Jospin should want time to consider the text of the stability pact before it was formally adopted.

Another note of uncertainty in moves towards EMU has been injected by a row between Bonn and the Bundesbank over plans to revalue assets, plus a jump in German unemployment, which have raised concern over how Germany would cut its deficit to three percent of GDP as required by EMU.
